title: How to Build a Cell Diagnostic Lab With Claude and Google Sites
author: Phillip Alcock
summary: Phillip Alcock gives teachers a step-by-step recipe for building a simulated cell diagnostic lab, called Bio-Vault, with Claude and embedding it in a Google Site. Students investigate four fictional cell samples, record readings in a notebook and write a clinical pathology report as a four-part biology micro-project. The post supplies the full prompt to paste into Claude, explains what the HTML, CSS and JavaScript each do so a teacher can inspect the result, and walks through testing the embedded app on the published site. Its design choices are pedagogical as much as technical: deterministic results so students can compare evidence, a baseline and post-test reading, and a notebook that asks for explanations rather than organelle names. It also builds in safeguards, including fictional patient data, a visible warning about browser storage and a copyable text report. The piece is a practical workflow for classroom teachers rather than a general AI tutorial, so it sits in Ed-Tech.
points: Deterministic simulated results (the same test on the same specimen gives the same reading) are what let students compare evidence and defend a diagnosis.
The notebook is designed to make students explain how cell structures work together, using a baseline and post-test reading rather than naming organelles.
Teachers should inspect and test the generated app on the published Google Site, since clipboard and storage features can behave differently from the preview.
Safeguards matter: use fictional patient names, label the data as invented teaching models, and have students copy work into their own document.
quotes: Students investigate four fictional cell samples, record evidence and use their findings to write a clinical pathology report.
Use fictional patient names and symptoms. Ask students to leave their own names and other identifying information out of the app’s notebook.

The app needs a consistent set of results. If students run the same test on the same specimen twice, they should see the same reading. Otherwise, they cannot compare evidence or explain their diagnosis.
The cases are simplified models. For example, a fluorescent tracer in the app represents the movement of a protein through a cell. The display does not reproduce a real laboratory assay.
It also asks students to describe a connection between cell structures, rather than naming an organelle without explaining its role.
Claude can attempt to save notes in the browser using local storage. That storage belongs to a particular browser and device, and it may be unavailable or cleared.

Google Sites supports embedded HTML, CSS and JavaScript. The code remains inside the embedded area, so features such as copying to the clipboard or saving notes need to be tested in the published site as well as in Claude’s preview.
